lessons.title: Introductions and small talk
lessons.tip: At work, start with a friendly greeting, your name and your role: “Hi, I’m Lena. I work in finance.” Small talk builds trust. Ask an open question about the other person, listen, and share a little about yourself. Keep the topics light: the weather, your commute, the weekend, your work.

lessons.title: Meetings: agree, disagree, interrupt
lessons.tip: In meetings, agree and disagree politely. To agree: “I agree with that,” “That makes sense.” To disagree gently: “I see it a little differently,” “I’m not sure about that.” To interrupt politely: “Sorry to interrupt, may I add something?” Keep your tone calm.

lessons.title: Write a clear email
lessons.tip: A clear email has a short subject line, a greeting, the main point in the first sentence, any needed details, a clear request with a date, and a polite closing. Keep sentences short. One email, one topic.

lessons.title: Status updates: BLUF
lessons.tip: BLUF means Bottom Line Up Front. Start with the result or the decision, then give the reasons and details: “The report will be one day late. The data arrived on Tuesday. I will send it by Friday.” Busy readers get the key point at once.

lessons.title: PREP answers
lessons.tip: PREP is a simple structure for answering questions: Point (your answer first), Reason (why), Example (a short real case), Point (your answer again). “Remote work suits me, because I focus better. Last year I finished a report early at home. So I work well remotely.”

lessons.title: Interview answers with STAR
lessons.tip: For “Tell me about a time…” questions, use STAR: Situation (the background), Task (your job), Action (what you did) and Result (what happened). Say “I,” not “we,” for your own actions. End with a clear, positive result, and add a number if you can.

lessons.title: Plain language
lessons.tip: Plain language means writing so your reader understands at the first reading. Use short sentences, everyday words, active verbs and “you.” Replace “utilize” with “use” and “commence” with “start.” Cut extra words.

lessons.title: Feedback with SBI

lessons.title: Run a meeting well
lessons.tip: A good meeting has a purpose, an agenda and a time limit. Send the agenda in advance. Start on time, state the goal, and give each point a time. During the meeting, keep to the agenda: “Let’s park that and come back to it.” At the end, summarize decisions and name who will do what by when. Send notes the same day.

lessons.title: Push back politely
lessons.tip: Sometimes you need to say no, or not yet, to a request. Start with the shared goal, then give the limit and an option: “I want to help the launch succeed. I can’t finish it by Friday, but I can have a first version by Tuesday.” Offer choices instead of a flat refusal. Use “can’t” for a real limit and “prefer” for a choice. Stay calm and specific.
sources: Common workplace-communication practice: agendas, action items and clear requests (concepts only; original wording)

lessons.title: Present data with a message
lessons.tip: When you present numbers, lead with the insight, then show the proof. “Our new plan sells better after the price change” is stronger than “Here is a chart of sales.” Use one message per chart and point to the key number. Say what it means for the listeners: “So we should keep the lower price.” End with a recommendation or a question.

lessons.title: Raise a problem clearly
lessons.tip: To raise a problem, use three parts: the problem, the impact, and your request. “The shipment is late (problem). We cannot start training on Monday (impact). Could you approve a different supplier by Wednesday? (request).” Stick to facts, say what you already tried, and make the request specific, with a date. Avoid blame; focus on the fix.
sources: Common workplace-communication practice: agendas, action items and clear requests (concepts only; original wording)

lessons.title: Follow up without nagging
lessons.tip: A good follow-up is short, polite and easy to answer. Remind the person what it is about, ask one clear question, and give a date. “Could you confirm the 12th or the 19th by Thursday?” is easier to answer than “Any news?” Thank the person. If you still hear nothing, wait a few days and follow up once more with a new angle, not a louder one.
sources: Common workplace-communication practice: agendas, action items and clear requests (concepts only; original wording)
Plain English guidance for professional writing (ideas only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Receive feedback
lessons.tip: Feedback can feel personal, but it helps you grow. Listen without interrupting. Ask a question to understand: “Could you give me an example?” Summarize what you heard: “So you’d like shorter updates.” Thank the person, then decide what to change. You do not have to agree with everything, but respond with respect. Follow up later and show the change.

lessons.title: Map and align stakeholders
lessons.tip: A good idea fails when the wrong people hear about it late. List the stakeholders: who decides, who is affected, who can block. For each, note what they care about and what they fear. Speak to the key ones before the meeting, so the meeting confirms instead of surprises. Use their language: finance cares about cost and risk, operations about workload, customers about service. Ask for objections early; an early “no” is cheaper than a late one.

lessons.title: Write an executive summary
lessons.tip: Executives read the first lines and decide how much more to read. An executive summary leads with the recommendation, then gives the reason, the risk and the decision needed, with a date. Use numbers, not adjectives: “cost us 400,000 dollars” rather than “cost us a lot.” Keep it to one page. Everything in the summary must also appear, supported, in the body. Remove background that a decision-maker already knows.

lessons.title: Make the ask: value, risk and return
lessons.tip: When you ask for money, time or authority, make it easy to say yes. State the ask first and specifically: “I am requesting 50,000 dollars to pilot the system for six months.” Show the expected return and how you will measure it. lessons.tip: Bad news and performance problems need preparation. Choose a private time and a calm place. lessons.title: Work across time zones and cultures
lessons.tip: Global teams need explicit habits. Choose meeting times that rotate the inconvenience. Send the agenda and materials in advance, so non-native speakers can prepare. Use plain, specific dates: “Friday 12 June, 5 p.m. London time.” Record decisions in a shared place.

lessons.title: Precise language in agreements
lessons.tip: Contracts and formal agreements need precise language. Shall states an obligation; may states permission; must states a requirement. Avoid vague words like “promptly” or “reasonable” unless they are defined. Specify who does what, by when and what happens if it is not done. Define terms once and use them consistently. This is language practice, not legal advice: for real contracts, ask a qualified lawyer.

lessons.title: Communicate in a crisis
lessons.tip: In a crisis, speed and honesty matter. Say what happened, what you know, what you do not know yet and what you are doing about it. Apologize clearly when you are responsible, without excuses. Tell affected people directly and first, then the public. Give an update time even when there is no news: “We will update you at 3 p.m.” Do not speculate or blame. Afterward, explain what you will change.

lessons.title: Answer tough questions in public
lessons.tip: In a panel or press Q&A, answer the question briefly, then bridge to your key message. Bridging phrases: “What matters most is…” and “The important point is…”. Do not repeat a negative word from the question: if asked “Is the product failing?”, do not say “The product is not failing”; say what is true. If you do not know, say so and offer to follow up. Never say “no comment.” Keep answers short and prepare three key messages.
